Original review snapshot

The assessment and source excerpts below are retained as the rationale for these changes. Their old-behavior descriptions and line numbers describe the pre-fix snapshot, not the implementation now installed.

Assessment

The central issue is allocation of attention. Fresh work always wins the first round, reading can repeatedly defer maintenance, and custom plans can multiply alerts. Fixing those policies is more valuable than adding further scheduling complexity.

Keep

  • Questions without answer spoilers in notifications.
  • Deferral during prayer windows and active reading.
  • Coalescing coincident slots and quietly removing resolved points.
  • Short five-point rounds and an accessible manual continuation.
  • Separate fresh practice from expanding long-term intervals.

Change first

  1. Align delivery and previews with the real schedule.
  2. Guarantee overdue checks room in each mixed session.
  3. Set one shared interruption policy, including late catch-up.
  4. Make exposure deferral and schedule ownership understandable.

What the strategy does today

StageCurrent rulePractical meaning
Fresh mistakeAuto: 3 recalls for the first slip, 4 for the second, 5 from the third lifetime slip. A currently mastered point gets 2 only below that third-slip threshold. Light: 1. Intensive: 5.Successful unaided recalls reduce the target; hesitation keeps the remaining fresh count; a new mistake restarts the phase.
Eligible again45 minutes after the last exposure/answer, or an earlier intervening prayer-window end.This is eligibility, not an automatic 45-minute notification. Delivery still waits for a selected reminder slot.
Long-term checksIntervals of +1, +3, +7, +14, +30, +60 days; then +60 repeatedly, measured from successful checks.On-time cumulative dates after fresh completion: day 1, 4, 11, 25, 55, 115. ثبتت is reached after passing the 14-day-interval check; future maintenance continues.
ExposureFresh checks get a renewed wait; spaced checks seen/heard today wait until a later calendar day.Reading is not credited as an unaided answer.
NotificationsFresh points use their own times or global times. Spaced checks use global times, at most once per prayer day. The default has all five prayer slots.Not every slot produces an alert. Fresh due work can trigger repeated slots; private schedules can add more.
Session sizeUp to five points, ordered fresh-first, then care needs and due date, with safeguards against exposing another answer.Round size is bounded; total daily work and combined alerts are not.

The ladder is in Hifz.kt:450–499; targets, exposure, scheduling and session selection are reproduced in the evidence below. “Mastered” here describes the app’s state, not a measured guarantee of permanent retention.

Findings

Two correctness defects are distinguished from intentional policies that deserve improvement. Examples describe conditions under which the source behavior matters; they are not claims that the Pixel 6 reproduced them.

  1. R01 · A daily point can join the previous day’s delayed Isha
  2. R02 · The plan can promise the wrong first reminder
  3. R03 · Fresh mistakes can crowd out overdue maintenance
  4. R04 · A daily reading routine can keep postponing a check
  5. R05 · Reminder frequency has no shared ceiling
  6. R06 · A missed morning reminder can arrive late at night
  7. R07 · Lifetime slips outweigh successful recovery
  8. R08 · The precise counts and prayer shortcut are heuristics
  9. R09 · The scope of a verse’s schedule is hard to predict
R01P2 · source defect

A daily point can join the previous day’s delayed Isha

Scheduling respects a daily point’s due day, but delivery checks the matching time and whether that prayer day already notified it. Delivery does not also require the reminder’s prayer day to reach the point’s due day.

Example

Manually answer a daily Isha point at 23:00; it remains fresh and is due tomorrow. Another point keeps that prayer day’s Isha reminder scheduled for 00:32. After midnight, the first point is calendar-day eligible and can join yesterday’s Isha, instead of waiting for tomorrow’s Isha. This requires no prior daily notification marker for that point.

Recommendation. Use the same prayer-day eligibility rule in scheduling and delivery. For daily fresh points, require the slot day to be at least dueDay as well as later than daily_asked.

Source-traced defect; not newly reproduced on the Pixel 6.

R02P2 · source defect

The plan can promise the wrong first reminder

The plan explanation sorts mixed prayer and clock times using fixed prayer estimates, including Fajr at 05:30. Delivery uses the actual local prayer window.

Example

Choose Fajr and 05:00. If the real after-Fajr slot is 04:50, the dialog names 05:00 as the first reminder, while delivery chooses after Fajr. Season, location, and prayer-window settings can all change the real ordering.

Recommendation. Generate the preview from the same schedule resolver as delivery. If no actual date/time is resolved, say “at your first selected reminder” instead of naming an estimated slot.

Source-traced mismatch between preview and delivery.

R03High · review balance

Fresh mistakes can crowd out overdue maintenance

Every fresh point ranks ahead of every spaced check. A notification selects at most five points, then marks the eligible spaced-check day reminded even if none of its checks fit in that batch. Opening the notification normally starts with those five IDs.

Example

Five persistent fresh points and ten overdue spaced checks are eligible. The learner completes only the notification’s first round and continues adding or struggling with fresh points. Old checks can repeatedly remain behind the fresh work; later fresh-only reminders do not re-add that day’s spaced checks. The notification does mention that more points exist.

Recommendation. Reserve capacity for overdue spaced checks and rotate unfinished work. For example, trial three fresh points plus two overdue checks when both exist, redistributing unused places and preserving answer-exposure ordering. Keep unserved checks eligible without creating extra alerts. The 3/2 split is a proposed starting policy, not a validated learning optimum.

Deterministic consequence of the selection policy; the learner behavior is an illustrative scenario.

R04High · review availability

A daily reading routine can keep postponing a check

A spaced check is excluded for the rest of any calendar day in which its verse was deliberately seen or heard. The next day clears that exclusion, but new exposure applies it again. This protects unaided recall from recently seeing the answer.

Example

The learner reads or listens to the same passage before opening review every day. Its overdue checks can stay unavailable day after day even though the learner regularly uses the app.

Recommendation. Preserve the exposure safeguard, but offer a review-first entry before reading a due passage. Clearly show which checks were deferred and why. If a later same-day check is introduced, define and evaluate its separation rule rather than silently treating reading as successful recall.

Source-confirmed daily exclusion; indefinite deferral depends on the repeated routine described.

R05High · interruption load

Reminder frequency has no shared ceiling

The default enables all five prayer slots. Fresh points can contribute different private schedules, and there is no combined daily alert budget, minimum alert spacing, or dismissal-based backoff. The six-clock limit is per schedule editor, not a limit across all points.

Example

Several fresh points with different custom times can produce more than eleven distinct daily alert opportunities when work remains due. A five-point round limits the size of each session, but not interruptions or total daily effort. Spaced checks alone are reminded once per prayer day.

Recommendation. Offer one preferred daily review slot as the starter choice, with three or five slots as explicit options. Add a shared interruption budget, coalesce nearby reminders, and expose “later” and “pause today.” Treat the budget and exact default as product choices to evaluate. Avoid silently changing schedules already chosen by existing users.

Source-confirmed absence of a global budget; actual alert count depends on due work and distinct schedules.

R06High · predictable timing

A missed morning reminder can arrive late at night

An overdue alarm remains owed. The three-hour stale rule drops it only when later slots cover all its work. A once-daily fresh point deliberately prevents that replacement, so a very late alarm can still alert. There is no separate nighttime catch-up boundary in this reminder path.

Example

The phone delays a morning-only reminder until late evening, or a long reading session releases an owed reminder on closing. Delivery may occur then rather than at the next chosen daily slot.

Recommendation. Define an explicit catch-up window and quiet hours. Outside the permitted window, keep the review due in the app and wait for the next chosen slot. A grace window such as 60–90 minutes is a candidate to test, not a research-backed threshold.

Intentional source behavior; exact background timing was not tested on a device in this review.

R07Medium · relearning effort

Lifetime slips outweigh successful recovery

Auto selects five recalls at three lifetime slips before checking whether the point was mastered. Every new “Again” restarts fresh learning and the spaced ladder. A long successful history therefore does not reduce the target once that lifetime threshold is crossed.

Example

A verse recovers from one relapse, passes many spaced checks, then has another lapse months later. Its third lifetime slip requires five fresh recalls, despite the recovery history. This may be appropriate for persistent trouble, but the current rule cannot distinguish it from an isolated late lapse.

Recommendation. Base relearning effort on recent difficulty and the strength/recency of successful checks, while retaining the learner’s explicit lighter or intensive choice. Present the target as a suggestion. Evaluate changes against delayed unaided recall and completion effort before claiming improvement.

Source-confirmed rule; the effect on learning or motivation has not been measured.

R08Medium · evidence and calibration

The precise counts and prayer shortcut are heuristics

Source comments characterize three recalls as best supported, more than five as adding little, and a prayer in between as equivalent to the 45-minute wait. The prayer shortcut uses configured prayer spans; it does not observe whether the learner prayed or forgot the answer.

Example

An answer is exposed just before a short configured prayer window. Its end can make a fresh point eligible well before 45 minutes, and a successful response advances progress. That may suit a routine, but is not proof of durable recall.

Recommendation. Describe the numbers and prayer exception as research-informed product defaults requiring validation. Separate prayer-friendly notification timing from the decision that a recall is sufficiently delayed. Keep the current simple ladder unless evaluation justifies a more complex model.

Code verified; the cited 2011 study’s original abstract was verified. The exact 2009 five-recall claim remains unverified. See the research section.

 126  /**
 127   * Right answers a first slip needs, each at its own reminder, before its checks space out: about 3 recalls before
 128   * spacing is the best-supported number (Rawson & Dunlosky 2011). A slip that comes back needs more; see [hifzAutoRecalls].
 129   */

 132  const val HifzMaxRecalls = 5

Hifz.kt:156–186

 156  /**
 157   * The least time between a fresh point's slip or answer and its next question: long enough that the answer is
 158   * recalled, not still in mind. A prayer prayed in between is enough too: see [hifzWaitEnd].
 159   */
 160  const val HifzFreshGapMs = 45 * 60_000L
 161  
 162  /**
 163   * A prayer, as the reminder of «المراجعة» keeps clear of it: from its adhan, or the start of its silence when that comes
 164   * first, to [end] (exclusive), when the reminder after it comes. The silence as the reader set it, also for a prayer
 165   * the app does not silence. A Friday's Dhuhr is the Jumu'a.
 166   */
 167  data class HifzPrayerSpan(val prayer: Prayer, val start: Long, val end: Long)
 168  
 169  /** The reader's prayers, for the reminder's times and a fresh point's wait; none until the app gives them, as in tests. */
 170  object HifzPrayerSpans {
 171      /** The prayers of the prayer days around [at], from the day before to the day after. */
 172      @Volatile var around: (at: Long) -> List<HifzPrayerSpan> = { emptyList() }
 173      /** The prayers that may end a wait from [from]: [around], unless the app knows that wait is over anyway. */
 174      @Volatile var forWait: (from: Long) -> List<HifzPrayerSpan> = { around(it) }
 175  }
 176  
 177  /**
 178   * When a fresh point whose answer was last in mind at [from] may be asked: [HifzFreshGapMs] later, or once a prayer
 179   * that began after [from] is over, when that comes first. A prayer in between takes the answer out of mind as the wait
 180   * does, and a strict wait would pass over that prayer's reminder for the next one, hours later.
 181   */
 182  fun hifzWaitEnd(from: Long): Long = hifzWaitPrayer(from)?.end ?: (from + HifzFreshGapMs)
 183  
 184  /** The prayer that ends the wait from [from] before [HifzFreshGapMs] is up; null when none does. See [hifzWaitEnd]. */
 185  fun hifzWaitPrayer(from: Long): HifzPrayerSpan? =
 186      HifzPrayerSpans.forWait(from).filter { it.start > from && it.end < from + HifzFreshGapMs }.minByOrNull { it.end }

 203       * or a Friday's khutba; to 20 minutes after the adhan when no window is known; never less than 10 minutes after it.
 204       * On Friday, Dhuhr is the Jumu'a; at a Tunisian place, the Eid prayers come too, as their silences set them. A

 215                  Prayer.entries.associateWith { PrefsManager.getSilenceRule(context, it) },
 216              ).windowsOf(date)

R09Medium · schedule ownership

The scope of a verse’s schedule is hard to predict

A global single-slot schedule is copied into a point’s private plan, including when saving a plan after changing only the recall count. Later global changes do not move that fresh point. Conversely, after fresh learning finishes, its spaced checks return to global times rather than keeping its private time.

Example

A user records a verse while the global time is 21:30, then changes global reminders to 20:00. That fresh verse can stay at 21:30. When it graduates to spaced checks, it follows the current global schedule. The UI explains the phase switch, but does not provide an explicit “follow settings” choice for this single-slot case.

Recommendation. Make schedule ownership explicit: “follow reminder settings” or “custom for this verse.” Track once-daily frequency separately from inheriting or overriding a time. Clearly label whether a custom plan covers fresh practice only or all future checks, and resolve previews using real times.

Source-confirmed intentional behavior; this is a predictability improvement.

A simpler reminder policy to trial

These are proposed defaults and acceptance criteria, not established learning-optimal parameters. Keep existing user selections during any migration.

Ask for a preferred daily review time. Offer prayer-relative or clock time; additional daily slots stay an explicit choice. Show the next real delivery time before saving.

Apply one shared alert budget. Merge nearby due work across all verse plans. Add “later” and “pause today,” and let the learner choose an effort target without hiding overdue work.

Mix fresh and overdue work. Reserve some of each five-point round for old checks, then fill remaining places. Respect answer-exposure dependencies when arranging the actual questions.

Handle missed slots predictably. Deliver within a stated grace period; otherwise use the next chosen slot. Keep pending work visible and honor quiet hours.

Protect review before reading. Offer due checks before the passage is exposed. Explain deferrals and the next opportunity instead of letting a check disappear from the learner’s routine.

Calibrate relearning with recent evidence. Keep a simple, explainable target and expanding ladder. Revisit targets using recent slips and successful delayed recall rather than lifetime failure count alone.

What the research supports

Retrieval practice and spaced relearning are a sound rationale; the app’s exact constants remain product heuristics.

Rawson & Dunlosky (2011) studied 533 students learning conceptual material. They compared 1–4 correct recalls during initial learning and 1 correct recall in each of 1–5 relearning sessions, with retention assessed 1–4 months later. Their efficiency recommendation combined three initial-session recalls with three widely spaced relearning sessions. This does not directly validate three separate prayer reminders before spacing, the adaptive 3/4/5/2 rule, or Quran recitation outcomes. Original article abstract via NCBI · Article DOI.

The identity of Pyc & Rawson (2009), Testing the retrieval effort hypothesis, was verified, but the source comment’s “beyond five adds little” claim could not be checked against the primary text. It is unverified, not disproved. Article DOI · Bibliographic metadata.

Neither verified evidence establishes a 45-minute threshold or a configured prayer window as an equivalent memory reset. Describe prayer timing as a useful routine and interruption constraint. Evaluate the learning rule separately.

Performed: current-source tracing across the model, delivery scheduler, exposure store, plan UI and notification entry point; independent reviews of scheduling and learning policy; primary-abstract verification.

Not performed: new builds, automated regression tests, timed notifications, Pixel 6 actions, or learning-outcome evaluation. No app source or existing device data was changed. The previous audit’s spaced-check duplicate and day-boundary corrections are still present; R01 concerns daily fresh points.

Acceptance cases for implementation

CaseExpected result after change
Daily Isha answered before midnight; previous prayer-day reminder arrives after midnightThe newly due point waits for its own eligible prayer day; unrelated overdue work can still be delivered.
Mixed Fajr and clock slots, across locations/seasonsThe displayed next reminder equals the delivery resolver’s earliest eligible slot.
Many fresh points and overdue spaced checksOld checks receive guaranteed capacity without revealing answers out of order or increasing the alert budget.
Read the same due passage before review on consecutive daysThe learner can see why checks are deferred and has a clear review-first opportunity.
Many private schedules and repeated dismissalsOne shared budget is respected; explicit postponement and pause are honored.
Morning-only alarm delayed until nightThe grace/quiet-hours policy is respected; due work remains visible for the next selected slot.
Change global time after saving a verse planInherited plans follow the change; custom plans remain fixed and clearly identified.
Long successful history followed by a lapseThe target follows the documented recent-history policy and preserves the learner’s explicit choice.

For later Pixel 6 validation: rediscover and explicitly target the device, take a fresh backup before testing, and compare persistent learning and settings data afterward. A previous backup must not replace newer user data.
